Documentation → Safeguards → Overview

Safeguards and guard rails

The catalog of protections that stop SATOM from losing data, locking you out or writing something nobody approved — the six design rules every guard follows and a map of the guard groups.

👤 ForOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereBuilt into the product; there is no single page to switch them on or off
On this page
  • What the safeguards are for
  • The six rules every guard follows
  • Map of the guard groups
  • How to read the group articles

What the safeguards are for#

SATOM writes to production appliances, rewrites its own installation, installs its own dependencies and reloads its own web server. Every one of those is a way to lose data or lock yourself out. The safeguards are the guards that make those operations survivable.

Every guard described in this section ships in the product today. Most of them are invisible while they hold: you only see one when it refuses something, rolls something back or raises an alert.

❗Important — The failure this product defends against hardest

Not a missing guard, but a guard that silently takes the wrong branch and reports success. Several guards below exist because a step once returned success while doing nothing.

The six rules every guard follows#

Every guard in this section is built to the same six rules — each one a direct answer to a guard that could otherwise report success while doing nothing:

📣Fail loud

A guard that cannot do its job aborts the operation. No step is allowed to report success while doing nothing.

For example: an update aborts if local commits cannot be parked first, and publishing a manual stops the build on any leak-scan hit.

📸Snapshot first

Nothing destructive runs before the previous state is parked somewhere that survives the destruction.

For example: the current revision or library version is recorded before an update, and local commits are parked before a hard reset.

✅Verify, then commit

Every self-mutation — code, dependency, certificate — is followed by a real check: import smoke test, configuration test, HTTP health check. On failure it reverts automatically.

For example: a certificate import the web server rejects is rolled back and the server reloaded.

🔒Allowlist, never free-form

Package names, provider fields, document slugs, remote file names and device command verbs are closed sets, re-validated at the privileged end.

For example: there is no "install any package" path from the browser — only the application's own library inventory.

✍️One writer

On a two-node cluster the primary owns every replicated write. The standby refuses rather than producing state its own synchronization would undo.

For example: updates, promotion and backup deletes are refused on the standby.

🎛️Operator edits outrank seeds

Tunable data is seeded insert-only into the database, so an upgrade never brings back something an operator deliberately removed.

For example: a corrected endpoint or provider row survives every deploy — and nothing is scheduled on your behalf after an install.

Map of the guard groups#

Group Covers Article
Code and updates Repository history, bundles, code and dependency updates with automatic rollback Code history and updates
Privilege boundary and operator console The unprivileged service account, the privileged update runner, and the satom console Privilege boundary and operator console
Two-node correctness Primary/standby rules that prevent split brain and undone deletions Two-node correctness
Writing to appliances Read-only commands, dry runs, lease locks, change-request gating Writing to appliances
Certificates and files from outside Certificate import rollback, ACME signing, renewal journal, name validation, checksums Certificates and files from outside
Sessions, web surface and appearance Security headers, CSRF, rate limits, lockout, 2FA, safe theming Sessions, web surface and appearance
Documentation and content Redaction of published manuals, offline manual, content that cannot be hidden Documentation and content
Monitoring and alerts Health badges that can turn red, scoping, silent-unless-failing work, the alert catalog Monitoring and alerts
Fresh installs and known limits What is armed from the first boot, what you must arm yourself, and the published limits Fresh installs and known limits

💡Tip — Start here after an install

Read Fresh installs and known limits first. The code-level guards are active from the first boot, but scheduled actions appear only with the first appliance and alert recipients are not created for you — an install without them is the most common way to end up unprotected.

How to read the group articles#

Each group article starts with a short explanation of the risk, followed by a Guard | What it prevents table. The right-hand column names the concrete failure the guard exists to stop — often one that actually happened. Where a guard has a limit, it is stated in a callout rather than left implied.

For the security model as a whole (accounts, permissions, encryption, audit), see Security model. For how the pieces fit together, see Architecture.
